newsitem.title: UK: BTPs, lira convinced Prodi govt to survive turmoil.
newsitem.headline: BTPs, lira convinced Prodi govt to survive turmoil.

text.p: Political risk has reared its head in Italy once again, threatening to shatter months of stability, but Italian markets are largely unruffled, confident the government will muddle through, economists said on Tuesday.

BTPs (Italian government bonds) -- which have blossomed under months of political calm and hopes of joining a single European currency -- may see some volatility in the short run, but medium term can narrow further the yield gap on Bunds further, they said.
"We tend to down play the significance of this political crisis," said CS First Boston economist Francesco Giordano.
"Nobody really believes that it is going to break the government. The general consensus is that it is more stable than the newspaper headlines suggest."

Italy's centre-left government, with coalition members at loggerheads on foreign policy, readied itself on Tuesday for a parliamentary vote on sending an Italian-led mulitnational security force to Albania.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's coalition partner the Communist Refoundation party said on Monday it would oppose plans to send the military mission to Albania.
And the main centre-right opposition Freedom Alliance upped the ante on Tuesday by saying it would also vote against the government in Tuesday and Wednesday's ballots.
But analysts, who have seen Italian political crises come and go, said the wrangling would fall short of toppling the government.
"The worse to expect is that the government will be defeated over Albania," said Rob Hayward, economist at Bank America here.
"I don't think, they will resign over this issue -- it would be suicide to have an early election."
Giordano, based in London, said one factor favouring the government was it may be able to separate the Albania issue.
"One positive thing about the Albania crisis is that although it is important for Italy, it can be isolated...it does not involve day to day issues," he said.
Adrian Owens, European economist at Julius Baer Investments in London, said political turmoil could spark periodic volatility for Italian assets but agreed the government would likely muddle through.
"There will be political scares and we will see volatility and occaisonal setbacks longer term, but if it wasn't for this coalition the Communist Refoundation wouldn't have a voice at all," he said.
"They're going to be very reluctant to cause the collapse of the coalition."

Hayward said BTPs had already seen most of the negative fall-out from the political turmoil. By 1400 GMT, the June BTP contract on LIFFE was down 30 basis points at 127.20. The 10-year BTP/bund spread was at 183 basis points, up from 175 at Monday's close.
"Unless things heat up and the government is defeated...I don't see the BTP/Bund spread going much further from where we are now," he said.

"There is a risk that the spread could go up to 200 basis points, but it would certainly look very cheap there, given the increased optimism in the last week about European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU)," said Hayward.
He said in the medium term, the spread could narrow to around 150 basis points.
Hayward said in the short term, the lira/mark may move to 990, but added medium term it would be steady in the 980 to 990 range. Mark/lira was at around 987/30/60 on Tuesday afternoon.
But even if Prodi does manage to weather the present political storm, he is by no means home and dry, analysts said.
"The danger is that this sets a precedent," said Giordano.

"It's quite clear in the way the 1997 mini budget was constructed that the government wants to press ahead with fundamental reforms in the spring or early summer...so the risk of more serious political confrontation is quite strong."
Owens agreed pension and welfare reform could be two other potential political minefields.

"The other issue is of course whether Italy needs to make adjustments to meet the EMU criteria and ultimately in May of next year if Italy is not given first round memebership Prodi is on record he will resign," he said.
"But in the short-term it would cause me to start selling my Italian assets."
